The past couple of weeks have been randomized rotation, frustration, and chop. You get traction for a few days and then it's gone. You have to be quick to rotate, act and react.

One thing stays consistent though. If you start system hopping or go way outside what you're used to doing, your results aren't going to reflect that the way you hope. Every time you change a strategy or change how you trade, there's a period where you're adapting to the new way of doing things.

For me that's always hurt more than it's helped.

When you add new components to your trading, take the time to master each one. If you're carrying too many pieces you haven't mastered and you're making it up on the fly, the outcomes get variable, random and frustrating.

Speaking to top traders over the past few years, they split about evenly on this.

Half of them swear by the psychological side. They've mastered pattern recognition, they can flip through charts and see it instantly, so what's left is managing themselves.

The other half says psychology is the excuse you reach for when you haven't studied enough. No scientific evidence it plays a role. Just study your setup until it's second nature.

My take is it's a bit of both. 

The longer you do this, the more patterns you've seen and the more cycles you've been through, the better you get. Maybe psychology matters less at that point. I agree with that.

But there's still the social media piece. I spoke to one trader this week who hasn't signed into Twitter since February. Doesn't want to see anyone else's opinion at all. For him that's the edge.

Some people improve by cutting out whatever hurts their psyche. Others by mastering every pattern and running it for 20 years straight. Do the same thing for two decades and of course you'll be good at it.

There's no right answer. It's whatever gets you to your end goal.
